purpose: Alogliptin is used to help control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It is used along with diet and exercise, and sometimes with other diabetes medicines. It is not used for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis.
how_it_works: Your body makes a hormone called incretin after you eat, which tells your pancreas to release insulin to lower your blood sugar. Alogliptin blocks an enzyme called DPP-4 that normally breaks down these incretin hormones too quickly. By blocking that enzyme, more incretin stays active longer, helping your pancreas release the right amount of insulin when you need it.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include stuffy or runny nose, sore throat, headache, and upper respiratory infections like a cold. Some people may also experience stomach upset or back pain. These are usually mild and tend to go away on their own.
warnings: Rarely, alogliptin can cause a serious condition called pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas) — stop taking it and call your doctor right away if you have severe stomach pain. It has also been linked to serious allergic reactions and a skin condition called bullous pemphigoid (painful blisters on the skin) — seek medical help immediately if these occur. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted. There is also a potential risk of heart failure, so let your doctor know if you have heart problems.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 25 mg taken by mouth once a day, with or without food. If you have kidney problems, your doctor may lower your dose. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes, and try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
